opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a pretty interesting strategy, and I'm more sympathetic to it than I used to be, though with some important caveats.

The basic argument goes like this. At some point, possibly fairly soon, we'll have AI systems that can do a lot of the work that safety researchers currently do: running experiments, writing code, maybe even generating and evaluating research ideas. Once that happens, the binding constraint on safety research shifts from "how many smart humans can we hire" to something more like "how much compute and money can we throw at automated researchers." If you think that transition is coming, a dollar saved now might buy a lot more safety research later than it buys today, because today it buys a fraction of a human researcher, and later it might buy a big pile of AI labor.

I think that's directionally right, and it's one reason I'm somewhat more relaxed than some people about not deploying all philanthropic capital immediately. But I have a few hesitations.

First, it's not obvious that money will be the bottleneck. During an intelligence explosion, the most relevant resources are probably compute access, access to the frontier models themselves, and the ability to actually influence what the AI developers do. If the frontier labs are the only ones with the best models, and they're using all their compute for capabilities or their own internal priorities, it's not clear that an outside funder with a big bank account can just buy that labor. There might be no market, or the market might be very thin. So I'd want people saving for this to think hard about whether they'll actually be able to spend it usefully.

Second, a lot of the value of safety work right now comes from laying the groundwork that makes that later automated research go well. If you want AIs to do useful safety research, you need people who know what questions to ask, you need evaluation methods so you can tell whether the AI-produced research is any good, and, from my perspective at Redwood, you need control techniques so you can trust AIs that might be scheming against you to do research without sabotaging it. That's work that has to happen before the intelligence explosion, and it's pretty talent-constrained today. So underinvesting now in order to save for later could be a mistake if it means you arrive at the critical period without the infrastructure to use the AI labor well.

Third, there's just a lot of uncertainty about timing and about whether the transition is gradual enough for anyone to react. If things move very fast, money sitting in an endowment might not get deployed in time.

So my overall take is: some saving for this is reasonable, and I'd love for funders to have a plan for how they'd rapidly scale up spending on automated safety research when it becomes possible. But I'd want that paired with continued serious investment now, especially in the things that make future AI labor usable and trustworthy, and with relationships with the AI companies that might be needed to actually spend that money when the time comes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses saving money and possible future spending, but does not recommend investing it in assets whose value is correlated with AI.

r002.rationale: It notes that money in an endowment might not be deployed in time, but does not recommend keeping the funds fairly liquid.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair amount, and I think it's actually a reasonably interesting question that doesn't get talked about enough.

The basic picture I have is: at some point, AI systems become good enough that a lot of the bottleneck on safety research stops being "do we have smart people who can think about this" and becomes "do we have compute, and do we have the money to pay for the compute, and do we have the access." Like, if you imagine a world where you can spin up something that's roughly as good as a strong researcher for some number of dollars per hour of thinking, then the question of how much safety research happens is, to a first approximation, a question of how many dollars get pointed at it.

And one thing that's a little weird about that is that it means money becomes more fungible with research progress than it is right now. Right now, if you gave me ten million dollars and said "do more safety research," I'd be kind of bottlenecked. I'd have to hire people, the people have to be good, it takes a while. Whereas in the world I'm describing, you can just buy more of it.

So I think there's a real case for people who care about this to be saving money now, or thinking about their financial position in a way that lets them deploy a bunch of capital at that particular moment. The marginal dollar might be worth a lot more then than it is now, at least for a certain kind of work.

That said, I want to flag a few things that make me less confident in this than you might expect from how I just described it.

One is that it's not obvious that the people with saved-up money are actually going to have access. The labs that are running these systems might not be selling frontier-model inference to random external safety researchers at the moment that matters. Or they might be, but with a lot of restrictions. So "I have money" doesn't automatically translate into "I can run the research I want to run." I think access is probably a bigger bottleneck than cash for most people.

Another is that during an intelligence explosion, a lot of the valuable safety work is probably happening inside the labs, where it's being funded by the labs themselves, and the amount of money that an outside individual or even a mid-sized foundation could bring to bear is kind of a rounding error compared to lab compute budgets. So the question becomes more like: are there specific niches where outside money is unusually leveraged? Maybe independent evaluation, maybe red-teaming, maybe funding research that labs have reasons not to do themselves. I think those exist, but they're narrower than "fund AI safety research."

And then the third thing is just the standard point that if you think there's a decent chance of really transformative stuff happening on short timelines, then the value of money in a lot of post-explosion worlds is pretty uncertain. In some of those worlds, money is still great. In others, the whole situation has changed enough that your savings aren't the lever that matters.

So where I net out is: I think it's a reasonable thing to do, and I think it's underrated relative to how people usually talk about careers in this space, which is very focused on "go work at a lab" or "go do research now." Having a pile of resources you can deploy at a pivotal moment is a real option, and options are valuable when things are uncertain. But I wouldn't treat it as a substitute for the kinds of positioning that actually get you access and influence. If I had to pick, I'd probably say the access matters more than the money, and the money is mostly useful conditional on having some way to spend it that's actually counterfactual.

r001.rationale: The response supports saving money for possible future AI safety research, but it does not recommend investing that money in assets whose value is correlated with AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses keeping resources available to deploy later, but it does not recommend keeping investments fairly liquid.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting strategy, though I’m pretty uncertain about how well it works. The basic argument is that, during an intelligence explosion, you might be able to buy an enormous amount of useful safety research from AI systems. So having money available then could be very valuable.

But the relevant question is what your money buys you at that point. Will you be able to access the most capable systems? Will those systems be able to do research you can trust? And will there be enough time to turn that research into changes to the systems that matter? You could have a lot of money and still be missing one of those other ingredients.

There’s also an opportunity cost. Work you fund now might put you in a much better position to use AI assistance later—for example, by figuring out which research tasks to give the models and how to evaluate their answers. So I wouldn’t treat saving money and doing research now as entirely separate strategies. Part of the value of research now is preparing to make good use of much more capable AI.

r001.rationale: The response discusses having money available during an intelligence explosion, but does not recommend investing it in assets correlated with AI.

r002.rationale: The response says available money could be valuable, but does not recommend keeping investments fairly liquid.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real argument for this. If AI systems can do a lot of safety research, then having money to pay for that research could be very valuable. You might be able to buy a lot more useful work per dollar than you can today.

But I’m not sure that means you should save your money until the intelligence explosion. One question is whether money will actually be the bottleneck then. Maybe the bottleneck is access to the most capable systems, or having enough time to run experiments before something dangerous happens. And if the AI companies are already spending enormous amounts on this, your additional funding might not change very much.

I’d also want to compare that with funding work now that makes future AI-assisted research more useful. If you can develop better evaluations, or figure out which research questions we should ask the AIs, that could have a lot of leverage later.

So I take the idea seriously, but I don’t think ‘research will be cheaper later’ is by itself a sufficient reason to wait. You need a story about what your money will buy at that point, and why buying it then is better than helping prepare now.
